chapter_theme: General songs (பொதுப்பாடல்கள், 7 of 21): the poet confesses the sea of lust and the women whose bodies he lists part by part, sees the body as a bag of gut, blood and worms, and fears Yama on his buffalo and the cremation fire; he asks for the feet, for song, and for the one Thing where speech and mind end, and rejects begging from patrons and the clamour of rival sects. The last five songs share a closing couplet on Murugan riding the peacock against the demons' elephants, chariots and horses.
structure_note: Pairs by meter and refrain: 1082-1083 (the sport with the millet-field girl), 1084-1085, 1086-1088, 1089-1090 (death and the gods freed from prison), 1091; then 1092-1096, whose praise is a long description of the peacock ending in the shared couplet கலபகக மயில் கடவி நிருதர் கஜ ரத துரக கடகமுடன் அமர் பொருத பெருமாளே. 1087 is an akam plea in a mother's voice.

1082.reading: Sunk in the sea of lust that swelled from dark infatuation, seeking fish-eyed women as if they were wealth, the poet fears the last day when Dharma comes on his buffalo with the tightened noose, and asks that before he is bound, he who thinks of Murugan as his help be given songs of verse and music. The praise names the hero who fights until enemies flee, the lord whose golden shoulders bear the Tamil songs and Vedas sung on earth, who rode the peacock round the world making the hill dust, and who joins the millet-field girl in sport.
1082.nuance: Yama is called தருமன், Dharma, the judge, rather than கூற்று. The plea is for இயல் இசை, verse and music: the gift of song as the poet's defence at death. பகர் தமிழ் பாடல் செழுமறை சேர் பொற்புயம: songs of Tamil and Veda as garlands on Murugan's shoulders.

1083.reading: The poet sees the body formed of earth, sky, wind and fire, where blood and semen join in the bag of skin with its foul gut, and asks that he not wander in this illusory birth suffering disease, but be given Murugan's holy feet bright with kadamba. The praise names the vel that ground Sura's army in the sea to dust, the lord of the three Tamils who chose many arts, the one who ran alone in play over the hill that the matted-haired one sought, and the one who embraces the doe-like girl.
1083.nuance: குருதியிலே சுக்கிலமது கூடி: the embryology of blood and semen, with the elements, makes birth itself the illusion (மாயப் பிறவி). The line on the 'bright sea' (கதிர்விடு வேலை) may name a shrine; the episode of the solitary play on the hill is not clear.

1084.reading: The poet confesses melting over the sandal-smeared, bodiced breasts of doe-eyed women whose eyes are like strife-making swords with poison set in them, and speaking words of helpless rapture; rather than perish so, he asks for the rising wisdom that speaks only of the grace of Murugan's two feet. The praise names him nephew of the old Mayan who sent the discus at the cry of the elephant seized by the crocodile in the pool, the grace of the huntress's breasts, and Murugan near to devotees whose vel broke the mountain.
1084.nuance: The cry of the elephant (பகடு வாய் விட்ட மொழி) is Gajendra's, as in 25. உதய ஞானம்: wisdom that rises like the dawn, and whose content is the feet's grace.

1085.reading: Listing the courtesans' eyes skilled in killing, their ear-rings, gait, oiled hair, teeth, breasts, slight waist, lotus face, back, forehead mark and parrot speech, the poet asks whether he should give his mind to these. The praise is a chain of names: master of arts, fierce Murugan, scourge of the wicked, the young, the golden, son of the mad one, praised god of the green peacock, the world, first of release, lord of siddhi, nephew of Vishnu, the One, the bright form garlanded with vetchi.
1085.nuance: Both halves are lists: the plea strings body parts with -இலே, the praise strings names with -னே, so the song sets the catalogue of women against the catalogue of the god. பித்தர் புதல்வனே, son of the madman, is Siva as பித்தன்.

1086.reading: Not content with the song of the anklets that fall at women's feet crying for refuge, as if the waist would break under breasts soaked in agil paste and musk, the poet asks to be granted to chant 'namah, refuge' to Murugan, who loves the girl of the forest dwellers who guards the millet on the hill. The praise names the lord who does not fear even at the end of the aeon, when the seven seas flood all the worlds, Brahma of the lotus and Mal, and the god on the great vermilion-faced elephant, perish and Hara dances with his consort.
1086.nuance: The cosmic dissolution (ஊழி முடிவு) is the setting of the praise: only Murugan stands unafraid when the gods go under. நம சரண் is a Sanskrit formula of surrender. Many compounds (பகலிரவு உண்டான இருவரும், லளிதவிர்) are hard to divide, and the identity of 'the two who made day and night' is unclear.

1087.reading: In a mother's voice, the singer asks that before her precious lightning-like girl wastes away, tormented by quarrelsome Kama's heavy flower arrows, the humming of bees drunk on honey, the sea's waves and roar, the moon that burns like the sun, and slipping conch bangles, Murugan dispel the darkness and embrace her with his red-garlanded shoulders. The praise shows the sun circling the world crying 'protect' and seeking Murugan, the vel that tore through Sura's head and shoulders, and the lord who once explained to the great one dancing with demons and ghosts.
1087.nuance: Akam convention throughout: the moon that burns (கலைமதி அங்காயும் வெயில்), the sea's roar and slipping conch bangles (சங்கு ஆளும்) are the classical tormentors of a girl in love. What Murugan taught Siva in the last line (அறமும் மறம் தோயும் அறிவு நிரம்பு) is obscure.

1088.reading: The poet sees the body as blood, water, skin, gut and bone, holding a life full of illusion, cruelty, anger and harsh lust, and asks that before Death comes with his long noose to take it and his mother cries out, he be given the art of joyfully chanting Murugan's grace, calling him Guha who rose from the lotus. The praise names the hero whose vel left great Sura's mind ruined and fleeing, and the one who once recited the ancient Veda that gladdened the Supreme who drank the poison and dances, praised by sun, moon and the one who dug up the earth.
1088.nuance: பழமறை அன்று ஓதும்: Murugan reciting the ancient Veda to Siva, the teaching story, without Om being named. The one who dug the earth (படியை இடந்தான்) is Vishnu as the boar.

1089.reading: Before everyone at home says 'take it, take it' of the body that heaps up both kinds of deeds and is ruined, weeps at the burning ground and lights the fire at its head, and before the riders of the dark, twin-horned buffalo tie their rope tight and call him, the poet asks Murugan to show him his pair of anklet-bound feet. The praise names him bridegroom of the hunter girl who drove off parrots, Kumara of the forehead eye that set old fire to the enemies' homes, the Murugan who listened in order to the Tamil song that set forth the Vedas, and the one who freed the gods.
1089.nuance: அருமறைகள் கூட்டி உரைசெய் தமிழ்ப் பாட்டை அடைவடைவு கேட்ட: Murugan as the listener to Tamil song that carries the Vedas, perhaps the hymns of the Saiva saints, though none is named. The forehead eye burning the enemies' homes is Siva's burning of the three cities; பகருநுதல் நாட்ட makes Murugan its son.

1090.reading: Before his kin are struck with grief, the body is laid on a high fire in the long forest of the dead, and Death binds his rope and strikes to bind the life, the poet asks for the mind to praise Murugan's feet with joy and eager longing. The praise names him the bridegroom who honours the feet of the girl with crescent brow and carp eyes, born in another form as child to the hunters to guard the millet, the one who gave knowledge to Siva of the matted hair with arugu, crescent, aththi and the Ganges, and the one who freed the gods.
1090.nuance: பிடியின் அடி போற்று மணவாளா: Murugan himself praises the feet of Valli, the she-elephant, reversing the poet's plea for Murugan's feet. பிறிது உருவில் வாய்த்து: Valli as a goddess born in another form among the hunters. அறிவீவாய்: the teaching of Siva.

1091.reading: Describing the union that women give, hair scattered, eyes closing, bangles jingling, sweet speech trembling and breasts pressed, the poet asks not to lose his mind in the cruel deceit of such women but to be given Murugan's two fragrant feet, the god who circled the world on his peacock in an instant. The praise names Rama whose arrow dried the sea, Krishna who fought the twin marutha trees, Hari who sleeps on the serpent with Lakshmi, Murugan's vel that scattered the demons, and the husband of the hunter girl, master of all arts.
1091.nuance: கலவி தரு மகளிர் கொடுமை எனும் உறு கபடம்: the scene ends in a judgment of deceit. The world-circling ride on the peacock is the race for the fruit, alluded to in passing.

1092.reading: The poet confesses singing to patrons, stuffing their names among titles like sinless, peerless, pure, steadfast, refuge-giver, Kama, Vijaya and Murugan, and telling each that his hand rivals the lotus, gem, conch, rain cloud, wish-cow and wish-tree, while they would not give a millet's worth; he asks for an end to the poverty of wandering from door to door, and for the one Thing where speech and mind cease. The praise describes the peacock, shining like gold, silver and emerald mountains, its shadow cast like the Vimala and Yamuna, spreading over Pothigai, and Murugan riding it against the demons' elephants, chariots, horses and armies.
1092.nuance: The poet's confession is of a court poet: the names of the god (முருகன் among them) wasted on men. மொழி ஒழிய மனம் ஒழிய ஒரு பொருள்: the remedy for begging is a silence where speech and mind end. The peacock lines are hard to divide.

1093.reading: The poet describes the body of gut, faeces and urine, flesh, fat, blood and pale mire, with countless worms writhing and blood oozing until it stinks, which women perfume with civet and adorn with shining jewels as they come to delude the world, and asks for the understanding in which love pours, deeds end, mind ends and darkness ends. The praise likens the peacock to a mountain, to the discus that rends enemies, to the conch, and to the cloud that grew to measure the sea-girt world, and closes with Murugan riding it against the demons' armies.
1093.nuance: The peacock is described with the emblems of Vishnu, discus, conch and the cloud that grows to measure the world (Trivikrama), so the mount takes on the uncle's form. The plea is a chain of endings (வினை ஒழிய மனம் ஒழிய இருள் ஒழிய).

1094.reading: The poet sets against a crore of rival faiths, clamouring with sharp arguments, blind to the one Thing, his plea that the mire of the two deeds go, the instruments of the mind be shaken off, death and wound end, and melting and drinking the word he gain daily the sight of wisdom to know Murugan's musk-fragrant lotus feet. The praise shows the peacock at the end of time, when the stars scatter like sparks and the seven nether worlds, the mountains and the elephants of the quarters melt, running to the sky's summit like the black smoke of the submarine fire that drinks the seas.
1094.nuance: பரசமயம் ஒரு கோடி குருடர் தெரிவரியது ஒரு பொருள்: the sects are blind to the One, as in 1078, where the poet has left them. The praise sets the peacock in the cosmic dissolution, as 1086 does for Murugan.

1095.reading: The poet tells of women whose diamond and emerald-adorned eyes, as if Kama and Death had joined to worship slaughter, carry poison to take young men's lives, and of how following their unfathomable ways he found no path out of the seven births; he asks Murugan to grant a little of his eyes' grace to take this suffering blind man as his servant. The praise tells of Ganesha, whose belly is filled with puffed rice, aval, lentils and the three fruits offered at his feet, and who wrote the whole story of the Kurus with his one tusk on the northern peak as the sage spoke, and of Murugan's peacock that circled the sea-girt world in a moment.
1095.nuance: The praise turns to Ganesha as the scribe of the Mahabharata (குருநாடர் கதை முழுதும் எழுதும் ஒரு களிறு) before naming Murugan's swift peacock, perhaps the race for the fruit between the brothers. மறலி விறல் மதனன்: Death and Kama joined in the women's eyes.

1096.reading: The poet describes lovemaking in full, the women's eyes closing, speech trembling, bangles jingling, sweat on the brow, the garland scattered and hair loosened, drinking their lips and plunging into the sea of passion on the bed, and vows that even then he will not forget Murugan's feet. The praise shows Siva's dance, the back of Muyalakan cracking, the nether worlds struck as one foot rises, the moon shaken from his crown and all worlds reeling, and Murugan dancing beautifully in ways that delight that Lord, before the shared close of the peacock against the demons.
1096.nuance: Unusually, the plea is not to be saved from women but a vow: அவசமுறுகினும் அடிகள் மறவேனே, 'even when I am lost in passion I will not forget your feet'. Whether the dancer delighting Siva at the end is Murugan or the peacock is not certain.

links.note: Both list the body's gut, fat, blood and flesh (குடர், கொழு, குருதி, தடி) to undo desire; the Naladiyar asks which part is the garlanded woman, 1093 shows women perfuming and adorning that same body.
Tirumular says the six sects do not see the God within the body; 1094 calls the crore of rival faiths blind to the one Thing.

The Kural says not asking even from glad givers is ten million times better; 1092 shows the poet who begged from patrons who gave nothing, and seeks the end of that poverty not in better patrons but in the one Thing.
In 1078 the poet says he has escaped the crumbling other faiths; 1094 says why: they are blind to the one Thing.

Sunk in the sea of lust that grows from dark delusion (கருமயல்), the poet sought fish-eyed women as if they were the real thing, or wealth (பொருள் என நாடி), until the last day. Kural 351 says a joyless birth comes from the delusion (மருள்) that takes what is not the thing for the thing (பொருள் அல்லவற்றைப் பொருள் என்று). The hymn is a case of the error the Kural names, with Death's noose as its end.

The song sees blood and semen join in the bag of skin and gut (குருதியிலே சுக்கிலம் அது கூடி), with earth, sky, wind and fire, so that the body rises in an illusory birth (மாயப் பிறவி), and asks not to wander in it. Tirumanthiram 460 says that in the womb maya joins her brood to the soul (கர்ப்பத்துக் கேவல மாயாள் கிளைகூட்ட) and karma takes hold. The Tirumanthiram gives the doctrine behind the hymn's word மாய for the birth it describes.

The poet melts over doe-eyed women whose eyes are like strife-making swords with poison set in them (விடம் எலாம் வைத்த கலகவாள் ஒத்த விழி). Kural 1084 says the eyes of the artless girl have a look that eats the life of those who see them (கண்டார் உயிருண்ணும் தோற்றம்). Both make the eye a killer; the Kural's lover admires it, while the poet asks to be saved from it by the wisdom of the feet.

After listing the women's lily-like kohl eyes (குவளையேர் மைக்கண்), ear-rings, gait, hair, breasts and speech, the poet asks, 'should I give my mind to these?' (சித்தம் விடலாமோ). Naladiyar 44 asks, 'shall I give way' (கவற்ற விடுவேனோ) when men call eyes water-lilies, carp or spears, and answers that an eye is like a scooped-out palm fruit. Both refuse the catalogue with the same kind of rhetorical question; the hymn answers it with a catalogue of the god's names.

Instead of the women's anklets crying for refuge, the poet asks to be granted to chant 'nama, refuge' (நமசரண் என்று ஓத) to Murugan. Tirumanthiram 1850 tells the reader to long for the Lord morning, noon and evening and to sow his name with 'nama' (நம என்று நாமத்தை விச்சுமின்). Both make the name joined to 'nama' the act of surrender.

In a mother's voice the singer lists what wastes her daughter: Kama's flower arrows, the bees' humming, the sea's waves and roar, and the moon that burns like the sun (கலைமதி அங்காயும் வெயில்). Kural 1228 says the herdsman's flute becomes a messenger of the burning evening (அழல்போலும் மாலை) and a weapon that kills. Both turn gentle sights and sounds into weapons against the separated lover, the stock torments of akam carried into the hymn.

The song sees the body as blood, water, skin, gut and bone (குருதி சலம் தோலும் குடலுடன் என்பாலும்) holding a life of delusion and lust until Death takes it. Naladiyar 46 lists entrails, fat, blood, bone, sinew and skin (குடரும் கொழுவும் குருதியும் என்பும்) and asks which part is the garlanded woman. The same inventory serves the Naladiyar against desire and the hymn as a prelude to death.

Everyone at home says 'take it' of the body, weeps at the burning ground and lights the fire at its head (எரிய எரிமூட்டி). Tirumanthiram 157 has the wailing kin turn back at the town's edge, pile the wood and light the fire (விறகிட்டு எரிமூட்டி), then plunge into the water. Both stage the same cremation step by step; the hymn asks to see the anklet feet before it comes.

Before his kin are struck with grief (உறவின் முறையோர்க்கும் உறுதுயரம் வாய்த்து) and the body is burned, the poet asks for a mind that praises Murugan's feet with longing (வேட்கை). Tirumanthiram 152 ends the body's collapse with the loving ones weeping and going away (அன்புடையார்கள் அழுது அகன்றார்களே). The kin's love ends at the pyre; the hymn asks for a love that is turned to the feet before it.

The poet describes union with women in detail, then calls it the cruelty and deceit of women who give union (கலவி தரு மகளிர் கொடுமை எனும் உறு கபடம்) and asks not to lose his mind in it. Kural 913 says the false embrace of women who sell themselves (பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம்) is like embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room. Both judge the embrace itself as a lie.

After confessing years of piling titles on patrons in song, the poet asks for the one Thing where speech and mind cease (மொழி ஒழிய மனம் ஒழிய ஒரு பொருள்). Tirumanthiram 1896 says silence is when speech and mind are both still (வாக்கு மனமும் இரண்டும் மவுனமாம்), and silent speech alone is only muteness. The pairing shows the hymn's remedy for wasted praise is not mere silence but the stilling of both.

The women's eyes are made as if Death and Kama had joined to worship slaughter (வதை பழக மறலி விறல் மதனன் வழிபடுதும் என), to take young men's lives. Kural 1085 asks whether the young woman's look is Death, an eye or a doe (கூற்றமோ கண்ணோ பிணையோ). Both put Death in the woman's eye; the Kural's lover marvels, the poet calls himself the blind man it has caught.

The praise tells of the elephant who is offered puffed rice, aval, lentils and the three fruits and who writes the whole story of the Kurus with his tusk on the northern peak as the sage speaks (முனி பகர வட சிகரி மிசை ... எழுதும் ஒரு களிறு). The first song of the book praises Ganesha with fruit, appam, aval and puffed rice in hand, who first wrote on the first mountain (முற்படு கிரிதனில் முற்பட எழுதிய). The two share the scribe on the mountain and the offerings, though song 1 makes what he wrote the three Tamils.

The poet describes lovemaking at length and vows that even when lost in passion he will not forget Murugan's feet (அவசமுறுகினும் அடிகள் மறவேனே). Kural 1125 has the lover say he would recall her qualities if he forgot, but he does not know forgetting (மறப்பின் மறப்பறியேன்). The lover's inability to forget is moved from the beloved to the god's feet, and kept even inside another love.

source_issues: 1089: corrupt glyph in லு஡ட்டு, read ஊட்டு (flagged by CORRUPT_CHARS).
1090: corrupt glyphs in வுடலு஡டே (read உடலூடே) and மறவோ஡க்கு, where ஡ stands for ர் (read மறவோர்க்கு) (flagged by CORRUPT_CHARS: 2).
1086: லளிதவிர் is probably a misspelling of லலித; the line is hard to divide.
Across the chapter a stray space after the vowel உ splits words at line starts (உ டலெழு, உ ரையடி, உ ருகி, உ லகனே, உ றவின்முறை); read as one word.
